judge_comment: A pull cord that starts a fixed 3-minute cycle is a very simple, retro mechanical interface, but the single fixed duration limits it.

title: Twist-and-Release Spring Timer
new_elements: Twist-and-release spring timer (Spring returns to zero automatically)
rationale: No need to reset the timer after use.
judge_comment: A mechanical spring timer that auto-resets is simple and cheap, but wind-up timers already exist on microwaves, so it is a modest step.

title: One-Button Digital Controller
new_elements: One-button digital controller (Cycles through simple auto presets); Auto presets (Button chooses a preset, not a duration)
rationale: Digital accuracy without a keypad or learning curve.
judge_comment: A single button cycling through presets is easy to use and cheap, but it is a familiar approach with limited control.

title: Voice Confirmation Yes
new_elements: Confirm by saying yes (Microwave asks and user confirms)
rationale: A yes/no interaction is simpler than knobs or menus.
judge_comment: Voice yes/no confirmation is easy but adds a speaker and speech recognition, and it is vague about how the cooking is actually set.

title: Gesture Wave to Start
new_elements: Gesture sensor (Detects wave to start or open); Wave to start and open (No touch controls needed)
rationale: A single gesture replaces all manual controls.
judge_comment: Wave-to-start is intuitive, but it risks false triggers and doesn't address selecting time or power, and a sensor is not cheaper or simpler.

title: Clap-to-Cook
new_elements: Sound trigger (Recognizes a simple clap); Clap starts default cycle (No buttons or knobs)
rationale: Clapping is an instinctive, no-learning trigger.
judge_comment: Clap-to-start is a playful, no-learning trigger, but it is prone to false triggers from ambient noise and a safety concern for a heating appliance, and the default cycle is limiting.

title: Popcorn Button Only
new_elements: Popcorn button (Dedicated one-touch popcorn cycle); Popcorn preset (Correct time and power for popcorn)
rationale: One familiar task needs one obvious button.
judge_comment: Popcorn buttons already exist on most microwaves, and a single-purpose device is too narrow to serve general use with no learning curve.

title: Beverage Button Only
new_elements: Beverage button (Dedicated one-touch drink warming cycle); Beverage preset (Correct time and power for drinks)
rationale: A single beverage button avoids all settings.
judge_comment: A beverage preset is common and easy to build, but a microwave with only this button is limited and not radical.

title: Leftover Button Only
new_elements: Leftover button (Dedicated reheat cycle for plated leftovers); Leftover preset (Safe default reheat)
rationale: The most common task gets a single no-thought button.
judge_comment: Reheating is the most common use, so one button is simple, but the cycle's mechanism is vague and it is not very novel.

title: Frozen Meal Button Only
new_elements: Frozen meal button (Dedicated cycle for frozen dinners); Frozen meal preset (Auto time and power for frozen meals)
rationale: One button handles a common packaged meal.
judge_comment: Frozen meal presets are standard, and auto-timing needs package knowledge or sensors that the idea does not explain.

title: Single Warm Button
new_elements: Warm button (Gentle warming cycle only); Warm preset (Low-power default warming)
rationale: One action for warming removes power and time choices.
judge_comment: A single warm cycle removes choices and is very simple, but it is slow and limited and does not cover cooking.

title: Blank Faceplate
new_elements: Blank faceplate (No numbers, labels, or secondary controls visible)
rationale: Removing visible complexity reduces perceived learning curve.
judge_comment: A blank faceplate hides complexity but doesn't say how users actually operate it, so it may increase confusion.

title: Tactile Braille Dial
new_elements: Tactile Braille dial (Raised food and time markers); Touch-only preset selection (No reading required)
rationale: Tactile markers help users operate without visual learning.
judge_comment: Tactile dial with raised markers is plausible and helps accessibility, but still involves learning marker meanings and isn't really a simplification for all users.

title: Combined Door-and-Cook Button
new_elements: Combined door and cook button (One button opens and starts); Open and start in one action (Fuses door release and cook start)
rationale: Fusing actions into one button makes operation nearly thoughtless.
judge_comment: Single open-and-start button is simple, but opening and starting are conflicting actions, and it offers no way to set time or power.

title: Automatic Portion Detection
new_elements: Camera portion sensor (Looks at food and estimates volume); Auto time and power by portion (Sets cycle from visual portion)
rationale: The microwave decides everything after seeing the food.
judge_comment: Camera-based automatic cooking removes all decisions, but estimating volume and food type reliably is technically hard.

title: Smart Plate with NFC
new_elements: NFC plate reader (Reads embedded plate tag); Plate tells microwave how to cook (No user settings)
rationale: Using the correct plate automatically runs the correct cycle.
judge_comment: NFC-tagged plates make the cycle automatic, though they require special dishware and limit flexibility.

title: QR Code on Food
new_elements: QR scanner (Scans QR code printed on packaging); Auto-cook from QR code (Reads exact instructions)
rationale: Scanning is easier than interpreting package instructions.
judge_comment: Scan-to-cook removes interpretation, but depends on packaging adoption and QR codes with cooking data; not really a substitution of cheaper parts.

title: Time-of-Day Auto Presets
new_elements: Clock-based auto preset (Suggests breakfast, lunch, or dinner cycle); Meal-time mode (Automatically picks likely preset)
rationale: The microwave chooses a likely mode, reducing user decisions.
judge_comment: Easy to build, but guessing the meal by time is often wrong and adds confusion rather than removing it.

title: Proximity Auto-Light and Auto-Start
new_elements: Presence sensor (Detects user standing in front); Auto-ready state (Lights up and prepares default cycle)
rationale: The microwave anticipates use, so the user does less.
judge_comment: Presence sensing is feasible, but a lit-up default cycle doesn't help with actual operation and risks unwanted starts.

title: Hot Food Button with Steam Stop
new_elements: Steam-stop hot food button (One button reheats until steam detected)
rationale: One button plus sensing replaces timer and power decisions.
judge_comment: One-button reheat with steam sensing replaces time and power choices, and the sensor technology already exists in some models.

title: No Power Knob Food-Type Dial
new_elements: Food-type dial (Dial selects food type, not power level)
rationale: Users choose a food type instead of abstract power numbers.
judge_comment: A food-type dial is intuitive and simple to build, though similar to existing auto-menu presets.

title: Auto-Defrost by Weight
new_elements: Weight-based defrost (Weighs frozen food and defrosts automatically); Auto defrost cycle (No time or power input)
rationale: Defrosting becomes a single automatic action.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto-defrost already exists on many microwaves, so it is useful for simplicity but not radical, and it is only loosely a substitution.

title: Voice Door Latch
new_elements: Voice door latch (Door opens on spoken command)
rationale: Opening by voice removes the need to find a button.
judge_comment: Voice opening is feasible but covers only the door, so it barely helps with operation and adds complexity.

title: Kick-Activated Latch
new_elements: Kick-activated latch (Gentle knee or foot press opens door)
rationale: Hands-free opening works even when carrying food.
judge_comment: A kick or knee latch is a clever hands-free substitute for a handle or button, though it is a minor part of operation and could trigger accidentally.

title: Single Start Any Time
new_elements: Start button (Starts a default one-minute cycle); Default one-minute cycle (Safe for any quick reheat)
rationale: One start button with a safe default is immediately usable.
judge_comment: A single start button with a safe default replaces the whole control panel and has no learning curve, but it is quite plain and a fixed one-minute run may not suit every food.

title: Auto-Cook by Food Smell
new_elements: Smell/volatile sensor (Detects aroma volatiles from food); Auto-detect doneness (Stops when food smells cooked)
rationale: Sensing doneness removes all timer and power settings.
judge_comment: Smell-based doneness sensing would remove all settings and is radical, but reliable volatile sensing in a hot, humid cavity is hard.

title: One-Button Auto-Cook
new_elements: Single Auto-Cook Button (One large button starts a sensor-driven cooking cycle.); Zero-Decision Cooking (The microwave determines time and power automatically.)
rationale: Eliminates timer and power choices so anyone can cook without learning controls.
judge_comment: Directly serves zero-learning-curve, but sensor-driven auto-cook buttons already exist and reliably determining time and power for any food is hard.

title: RFID Package Scan
new_elements: RFID Reader (Scans food package tags for cooking instructions.); Automatic Recipe Execution (Sets time and power from the package.)
rationale: Removes manual programming by letting the package tell the microwave what to do.
judge_comment: Package tags that program the microwave are plausible and clear, though they only work for tagged foods and need packaging adoption.

title: Voice-Open Door
new_elements: Voice Latch (Door opens when user says 'open'.); Hands-Free Access (No push button or handle needed.)
rationale: No learning curve: speech is universal and the door simply opens.
judge_comment: Voice opening is easy to grasp, but it addresses only the door and raises safety and noise issues; it is not really a substitution that makes cooking simpler.

title: Stationary Wave Stirrer
new_elements: Mode Stirrer (Rotating antenna spreads microwaves without a turntable.); Even Heating Without Placement (Food can be put anywhere.)
rationale: Users no longer need to learn turntable alignment or glass plate handling.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are real and already common, and they remove turntable handling, but they only marginally help operation simplicity.

title: Sand Timer Dial
new_elements: Hourglass Timer (Visual sand timer replaces mechanical clockwork.); Intuitive Time Display (Time remaining is visible as sand level.)
rationale: No numbers or knob turns: sand falling is instantly understood.
judge_comment: A sand timer is a very intuitive and wild substitute for the timer, but it is imprecise, fixed-duration and hard to integrate with power control.

title: Motion-Start Door
new_elements: Motion Sensor (Detects door closing and starts cooking.); Auto-Start on Close (No start button needed.)
rationale: Closing the door is the only action, so operation requires zero learning.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is intuitive, but it risks accidental starts and needs some way to set the amount of heating, so it only partly removes the learning curve.

title: Hotness Dial Only
new_elements: Hotness Dial (One dial from cool to very hot.); Outcome-Based Heating (Internal sensor maps hotness to time/power.)
rationale: Replaces time and power with a single familiar hotness choice.
judge_comment: A single hotness dial replaces time and power settings and is highly intuitive, though reliably sensing internal food temperature is hard.

title: Foot-Pedal Door Release
new_elements: Foot Pedal (Press pedal to open door.); No-Hands Door Opening (Door opens without locating a button.)
rationale: A pedal is a simple, universal action requiring no instruction.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is simple and useful when hands are full, but it addresses only door opening and not the main operation.

title: Fully Transparent Door
new_elements: Transparent Microwave Mesh (See-through door eliminates interior lamp.); Always-Visible Interior (No light button or waiting to see food.)
rationale: Users just look in; no need to learn how to turn on a light or open door.
judge_comment: A fully transparent door is not really feasible because of microwave shielding, and it barely affects operational complexity.

title: Steam-Sensor Stop
new_elements: Steam Sensor (Detects when food is hot.); Auto-Stop Cooking (Cooking ends when steam appears.)
rationale: No timer setting: user just starts and the microwave stops itself.
judge_comment: Auto-stop on steam removes timer setting and is plausible, as sensor cooking already exists, but it works poorly for dry foods or foods that don't steam.

title: Full-Power Single Switch
new_elements: Single On/Off Switch (Full power only, sensor stops when done.); No Power Selection (Removes 5-step power knob.)
rationale: One switch is the simplest possible control.
judge_comment: A single switch is very simple to use, but full power with an auto-stop sensor is a modest, not radical, change and may overcook some foods.

title: Weight-Sensor Cook
new_elements: Weight Sensor Plate (Weighs food and sets cook cycle.); Put-and-Go Cooking (No need to guess time.)
rationale: User just places food; no settings to learn.
judge_comment: Weight-based automatic cooking removes the need to guess times, though it is not entirely new and weight alone doesn't determine the right program.

title: Barcode Scanner Cook
new_elements: Barcode Scanner (Scans grocery barcodes.); Package-Driven Cooking (Looks up and runs cook program.)
rationale: Scanning is familiar from checkout; no microwave-specific learning.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning is familiar and automates programs, but it needs a database and doesn't work for leftovers or unpackaged food.

title: Iris Door Opening
new_elements: Iris Door (Circular aperture opens by touch or voice.); No Handle or Button (Door opens with a natural gesture.)
rationale: Opening is obvious and requires no push-button search.
judge_comment: An iris door is eye-catching, but it is mechanically complex, hard to seal against microwave leakage, and only addresses opening.

title: Kick-to-Open Door
new_elements: Kick Latch (Gentle bump opens door.); Instant Door Access (No fine motor control needed.)
rationale: A nudge is simpler than finding and pressing a release button.
judge_comment: A kick latch is unusual and easy to understand, but it risks accidental opening and addresses only a minor part of operation.

title: Food-Picture Buttons
new_elements: Picture Keypad (Buttons show pizza, popcorn, coffee, etc.); Visual One-Press Cooking (Press the picture of the food.)
rationale: Pictures remove text-reading and power/time learning.
judge_comment: Picture presets are easy to use and highly feasible, but they are already common on microwaves and only loosely follow the substitute operator.

title: Popcorn-Only Microwave
new_elements: Popcorn Lever (Single lever for popcorn.); Single-Food Simplicity (No other controls.)
rationale: One purpose means nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single-purpose lever is trivially simple, but it limits usefulness and the idea is not very novel.

title: Phase-Change Heat Regulator
new_elements: Phase-Change Plate (Absorbs excess microwave energy at set temperature.); Self-Regulating Heating (Food cannot overcook.)
rationale: No power levels: the plate automatically stops overheating.
judge_comment: A radical substitution of control with a passive self-regulating material, but physically doubtful and the plate would need to be well defined.

title: Voice Cook and Stop
new_elements: Voice Command Mic (Listens for 'cook' and 'stop'.); Two-Word Operation (Only two words needed.)
rationale: Two universal words replace all knobs and buttons.
judge_comment: Two-word voice control is simple, but it does not set time or power and noisy environments may cause problems.

title: Wave-to-Start Sensor
new_elements: Proximity Sensor (Wave hand to start.); Gesture Start (No button press needed.)
rationale: A wave is intuitive and requires no control learning.
judge_comment: Wave-to-start is easy but only covers starting, with no way to set time or power, and false triggers are a risk.

title: Glow-in-the-Dark Interior
new_elements: Phosphorescent Liner (Interior glows after door opens.); Light Without Bulb (No lamp or switch to learn.)
rationale: Interior is always visible without a light control.
judge_comment: Phosphorescent liner removes a lamp but interior lighting is not a real learning barrier, and the glow fades and may not be bright enough.

title: Integrated Egg Timer
new_elements: Door-Mounted Egg Timer (Twist dial on door, no separate clock.); Familiar Twist Timer (Uses a known kitchen object.)
rationale: Everyone knows an egg timer, so no microwave-specific learning.
judge_comment: Mechanical twist timers are already common on microwaves, so this is highly usable and feasible but hardly radical.

title: Reheat-Only Button
new_elements: Reheat Button (Single reheat button.); One-Touch Reheating (Sensor sets time and power.)
rationale: Most users only reheat; one button removes all choices.
judge_comment: A single sensor-driven reheat button removes choices and is plausible, but it limits function and similar sensor buttons already exist.

title: Spring-Open on Finish
new_elements: Spring-Loaded Door (Door pops open when cooking ends.); Auto-Open Notification (No bell or timer reading.)
rationale: The door opening itself is an unmistakable, zero-learning signal.
judge_comment: A door that springs open on finish is an intuitive signal that replaces the beep, but it does not simplify setting up a cook.

title: Pull-Lever Cook
new_elements: Pull Lever (Pull down to cook, release to stop.); Analog Dead-Man Control (No timer memory needed.)
rationale: Hold-to-cook is a universal physical metaphor.
judge_comment: A hold-to-cook lever is instantly understandable and needs no timer, though safety interlocks and tiring for long cooks are drawbacks.

title: Camera Outside Screen
new_elements: Interior Camera (Feeds a small outside screen.); See-Inside Without Window (No door holes or lamp needed.)
rationale: Users see food on a screen without learning anything new.
judge_comment: A camera and screen replace the window, but viewing food was never the learning barrier, and the camera would face heat, steam and splatter.

title: Single Transparent Panel
new_elements: Full Glass Front (Entire front is transparent mesh.); Unobstructed View (No small window or light.)
rationale: Looking inside is automatic and requires no control.
judge_comment: A fully transparent front mesh is vague and risks microwave leakage, and it does little to make operation simpler.

title: Moisture-Sensor Auto Cook
new_elements: Humidity Sensor (Detects food moisture loss.); Doneness Detection (Stops when food is ready.)
rationale: No time or power settings; the microwave decides.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensor auto-cook removes time and power settings, which directly serves the no-learning-curve need, though sensor cooking already exists.

title: Inverter Auto-Power
new_elements: Inverter Module (Continuously variable power without user control.); Automatic Power Modulation (Replaces 5-step power knob.)
rationale: Removes power-level learning entirely.
judge_comment: Inverter power is proven and removes the need to choose a power level, but it is already common and the user still sets a time.

title: Air-Driven Rotating Plate
new_elements: Air-Turbine Turntable (Microwave air currents rotate plate.); Self-Rotating Plate (No motor alignment or controls.)
rationale: Plate rotates automatically with no user action.
judge_comment: An air-turbine turntable is a creative substitute for the motor, but microwaves create little airflow, and users already never operate the plate.

title: Voice-Activated Latch
new_elements: Voice Latch (Door latch releases on voice.); Hands-Free Opening (No button or handle.)
rationale: Speaking is a natural interface with no learning curve.
judge_comment: Voice opening is intuitive, but it replaces a simple handle with a more complex and less reliable mechanism, and it does not address cooking operation.

title: Steam-Stop Only
new_elements: Steam Whistle (Mechanical whistle stops cooking.); Audible Auto-Stop (No electronics or timer.)
rationale: A whistle tells the user it is done without any settings.
judge_comment: A mechanical whistle is a quirky, simple substitution, but microwaves produce little steam and the user still has to decide when to stop, so it is only loosely workable.

title: One-Start After Close
new_elements: Door Switch Start (Closing door arms a single Start button.); Single Start Action (No mode selection.)
rationale: Only one button is ever needed: Start.
judge_comment: A single Start button armed by the door closing is very simple and easy to build, but it is not radical and leaves cook time undefined.

title: Temperature Dial
new_elements: Temperature Dial (Set desired food temperature.); Target-Temperature Cooking (Stops at set temperature.)
rationale: Temperature is a familiar concept from ovens and thermometers.
judge_comment: Target-temperature cooking is a familiar concept, but microwaves cannot easily sense food core temperature and it needs a probe or IR sensor.

title: Solar-Powered Timer
new_elements: Solar Cell Timer (No batteries or clockwork.); Maintenance-Free Timing (Always ready, no winding.)
rationale: Users never need to learn winding or battery replacement.
judge_comment: A solar timer removes maintenance but does little for operation learning, and it is poorly suited to indoor use and to a microwave that already has mains power.

title: Always-On LED Rim
new_elements: LED Rim Light (Soft light around door when closed.); No Light Switch (Interior visible when opened.)
rationale: No separate light control to discover.
judge_comment: Removes a trivial light switch but does little for the core learning curve of operating the microwave, and it is not radical.

title: Magnetic Voice-Open Door
new_elements: Magnetic Latch (Opens on voice command.); Effortless Door Release (No push button.)
rationale: Voice opening removes the need to find any button.
judge_comment: Voice-activated door release is plausible and easy to use, but it covers only opening, not cooking setup, and the voice interface is not a substitute for a button.

title: Sand Dial Power
new_elements: Sand Dial (Turn over to start, sand runs out to stop.); Visual Cook Timer (No numbers or beeps.)
rationale: Flipping a sand timer is an instantly understood action.
judge_comment: A flip-and-run sand timer is a radically simple, intuitive interaction, though it needs a mechanism to link sand flow to power on/off and gives imprecise timing.

title: Reheat and Defrost Only
new_elements: Two-Button Panel (Only Reheat and Defrost.); Two-Category Cooking (Covers most uses.)
rationale: Two buttons eliminate all other choices.
judge_comment: Two buttons nearly eliminate the learning curve and are easy to build, though similar simplified microwaves already exist and flexibility is reduced.

title: Rotating Antenna
new_elements: Rotating Antenna (Spins microwave beam instead of plate.); Even Heating Without Turntable (No plate to place or clean.)
rationale: Users never need to learn turntable positioning.
judge_comment: Rotating antennas (stirrers) exist and remove the turntable, but this does little for operation simplicity on the control side.

title: Gesture Control Pad
new_elements: Gesture Sensor (Swipe left to cook, right to stop.); Swipe Operation (Uses familiar touchscreen gestures.)
rationale: Swipe gestures are already learned from phones.
judge_comment: Swipe gestures are familiar, but a contactless gesture sensor adds cost and ambiguity, and it doesn't say how the user sets time or power, so it isn't truly simpler.

title: Auto-Door Open on Finish
new_elements: Auto-Open Hinge (Door opens when done.); Physical Done Signal (No bell or display.)
rationale: The open door tells the user food is ready without any learning.
judge_comment: The door opening as a done signal is intuitive and cheap, but it only covers the end of the cycle and not the operation itself.

title: Single Power Dial
new_elements: Single Power Dial (One dial from low to high; no timer.); Manual Power Only (User turns off when done.)
rationale: One dial resembles a volume knob, requiring no instruction.
judge_comment: A single dial is very simple and easy to build, but removing the timer shifts the burden to the user and it resembles old mechanical microwaves.

title: Clap-On Microwave
new_elements: Clap Sensor (Clap to start or stop.); Sound-Activated Operation (No buttons at all.)
rationale: Clapping is a universal, zero-learning trigger.
judge_comment: Clap activation is zero-learning to trigger, but it misfires on noise, and it doesn't cover setting time or power.

title: Timerless Keep-Warm
new_elements: Keep-Warm Sensor (Holds food at serving temperature.); No Timer Needed (Food never overcooks.)
rationale: User can ignore timing entirely.
judge_comment: Removing timing entirely is radical and well matched to the need, but sensing food temperature in a microwave is hard and the mechanism isn't specified.

title: Pull-Cord Start
new_elements: Pull Cord (Pull to start; let go to stop.); Physical Hold-to-Cook (No timer memory.)
rationale: A pull cord is a simple on/off action like a lamp.
judge_comment: A pull-and-hold cord makes operation intuitive and replaces the timer, but holding it for minutes is impractical and the safety/ergonomics are questionable.

title: Preset Pizza Button
new_elements: Pizza Button (One button cooks pizza perfectly.); Single-Food Preset (No time or power input.)
rationale: One picture button removes all programming.
judge_comment: A single preset button is very simple and easy to build, but it is limited to one food and is not radical.

title: Automatic Popcorn Sensor
new_elements: Popcorn Sensor (Listens for popping to stop.); Auto-Popcorn (No popcorn setting to learn.)
rationale: Popcorn cooks itself with no button except start.
judge_comment: Popcorn sensing already exists on many microwaves, so it is easy to build and useful but not novel.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Drawer Mechanism (Slide-out drawer instead of door.); No Door Latch Learning (Just push to open/close.)
rationale: Drawer action is familiar from cabinets and requires no instruction.
judge_comment: Drawer microwaves exist and make loading easy, but they do not simplify cooking controls, so the fit to the need is partial.

title: Single Serving Pod
new_elements: Pod Reader (Reads single-serve pod for auto cook.); Pod-Based Cooking (No settings, just insert pod.)
rationale: Like coffee pods, operation is simply insert and press start.
judge_comment: Insert-pod-and-press-start removes all settings and is a familiar model, though it needs a pod ecosystem and packaging that works in a microwave.

title: Color-Coded Heat Dials
new_elements: Color Dials (Blue, yellow, red for cold, warm, hot.); Color-Based Heating (No power level numbers.)
rationale: Colors are universally understood without learning.
judge_comment: Color dials replace numeric power levels simply and intuitively, but still require choosing a color and time, and are not very radical.

title: Touch Anywhere Start
new_elements: Any-Touch Panel (Whole front starts cooking when touched.); No Specific Button (Any touch triggers auto cook.)
rationale: Users cannot press the wrong button if any touch works.
judge_comment: Any-touch start removes button errors but risks accidental activation and safety issues, and doesn't address what or how long to cook.

title: Auto-Detect Food Type
new_elements: Camera Food Recognizer (Identifies food and sets cycle.); Automatic Food Recognition (No food category selection.)
rationale: The microwave recognizes food so the user does nothing.
judge_comment: Camera food recognition removes nearly all decisions, though it exists in some premium ovens and accuracy and cost are concerns, and it is more an addition than a cheaper substitution.

title: One-Touch Start Cube
new_elements: Single-action cook button (One press starts a fixed safe reheat cycle.)
rationale: Replaces duration setting with one obvious press, so no timer learning is required.
judge_comment: Directly removes timer-setting, but one-button microwaves already exist and a fixed cycle limits flexibility.

title: Fixed Two-Minute Bell Timer
new_elements: Fixed-cycle bimetallic timer (A sealed bimetallic strip always runs the same short reheat cycle.)
rationale: Substitutes the motor cam timer with a fixed-cycle element that users cannot mis-set.
judge_comment: A fixed-cycle mechanical timer is simple and mis-set-proof, though bimetallic timing is a bit odd and offers little flexibility.

title: Wave-to-Open Door
new_elements: Wave-to-open door sensor (A simple proximity gesture releases the latch automatically.)
rationale: Removes the push button and latch lever learning by making the door open on a hand wave.
judge_comment: A gesture door opener is feasible, but it adds cost and complexity and could cause false triggers or confusion.

title: No-Button Palm-Push Door
new_elements: Palm-push swing door (The door is held by a magnetic catch and pushed open directly.)
rationale: Substitutes the separate door button with pushing the door itself, which is instantly understandable.
judge_comment: Pushing the door open is intuitive, but a magnetic catch must also provide safety interlock and seal integrity, which is challenging.

title: Magnetic Self-Latching Door
new_elements: Magnetic self-latching door (A magnetic gasket holds the door shut and normal pull opens it.)
rationale: Replaces latch mechanics with a familiar fridge-like pull, requiring no button learning.
judge_comment: A fridge-like pull door is familiar and simple, but the magnetic gasket must meet microwave leakage safety and interlock requirements.

title: Doorless Microwave Drawer
new_elements: Pull-out microwave drawer (The cooking cavity slides out like a drawer with no hinged door.)
rationale: Eliminates door release and swing complexity, using only a familiar pull-out action.
judge_comment: A pull-out drawer is a radical, familiar action, but sealing microwave leakage and spill containment make it hard, and it only addresses door operation.

title: Voice-Only Cook Command
new_elements: Single-word voice command set (The only command is Cook, with automatic time and power.)
rationale: Replaces two knobs with one spoken word, making operation nearly self-evident.
judge_comment: A single spoken word needs no learning, but automatic time and power for arbitrary food is unreliable and voice recognition adds cost rather than simplicity.

title: One Rotary Action Knob
new_elements: One rotary action knob (Turning sets time and pressing starts; power is fully automatic.)
rationale: Collapses two controls into one physical action, reducing the interface to turn and press.
judge_comment: A single turn-and-press knob is simple and highly feasible, but it is an incremental simplification and not very wild.

title: Spring-Wound Egg Timer
new_elements: Spring-wound egg timer (A twist timer rings after a preset short cook without a motor or cam.)
rationale: Uses a universally familiar twist timer instead of an unfamiliar microwave timer knob.
judge_comment: A mechanical twist timer is familiar, cheap, and proven in microwaves, though it offers limited precision and is not very radical.

title: Color-Coded Food Buttons
new_elements: Color-coded food buttons (Five large colored buttons each run one safe preset.)
rationale: Replaces power-level abstraction with visual food categories that need no explanation.
judge_comment: Large color-coded preset buttons are intuitive and easy to build, but they are similar to existing preset-button microwaves.

title: Pictogram-Only Panel
new_elements: Pictogram-only control panel (All controls are pictures of food and actions, with no text or numbers.)
rationale: Substitutes written labels and numbers with universal icons for zero learning curve.
judge_comment: Icon-only controls reduce reading needs, but without numbers users lose control over time, and the concept is a modest, familiar step.

title: Tactile Braille Cooking Buttons
new_elements: Tactile Braille cooking buttons (Large raised-symbol buttons provide one-press presets by touch.)
rationale: Replaces visual timing and power settings with tactile presets that elderly users can feel.
judge_comment: Tactile presets help accessibility, but Braille is a questionable fit and raised symbols still have to be learned and don't add much.

title: One-Press Popcorn Button
new_elements: Popcorn-only button (A dedicated button runs exactly one popcorn cycle.)
rationale: Replaces manual time entry for the most common snack with a single labeled action.
judge_comment: Dedicated popcorn buttons already exist on most microwaves and cover just one use case, so it is simple but not radical.

title: RFID Meal Tag Auto-Cook
new_elements: RFID meal tag reader (A tag on the meal sets time and power automatically.)
rationale: Substitutes user programming with automatic tag reading, so nothing must be learned.
judge_comment: A tag that sets cooking parameters removes all operation, but it depends on food makers adopting tags and is impractical for generic food.

title: Barcode Scan Auto-Cook
new_elements: Barcode scanner (Scanning a package barcode sets a preset cook cycle.)
rationale: Replaces knob-setting with point-and-scan, matching a familiar grocery checkout action.
judge_comment: Scanning a barcode is familiar and could work using existing codes, but it needs a database and a scanner, and the scan is an extra step.

title: Weight-Sensing Auto-Time
new_elements: Load-cell weight auto timer (The turntable weighs food and derives a safe cook time.)
rationale: Eliminates duration decisions by sensing the food and choosing the time automatically.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto time is plausible and removes duration choice, but weight alone is a weak proxy for cook time and it isn't very radical.

title: Steam-Sensing Auto-Stop
new_elements: Humidity auto-stop sensor (A steam sensor ends cooking when food is hot.)
rationale: Substitutes a countdown timer with automatic doneness detection, so users only press start.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensor auto-stop is already common in sensor-cook microwaves and does reduce the user to pressing start.

title: Thermal Camera Auto-Stop
new_elements: Infrared food-temperature cutoff (An IR sensor stops the magnetron at target temperature.)
rationale: Removes timer guessing by stopping exactly when the food reaches temperature.
judge_comment: An IR temperature cutoff gives a direct doneness signal and is simple to use, but it only reads the surface, and the sensor adds cost and is hard to place inside the cavity.

title: Single Hot Food Button
new_elements: Hot Food button (One button reheats a typical plate with automatic power and time.)
rationale: Substitutes the entire two-knob interface with one button for the most common task.
judge_comment: One-button reheat presets already exist and are easy to use, but the preset is fixed and not radical.

title: Single Frozen Food Button
new_elements: Frozen Food button (One button defrosts and heats a typical frozen meal.)
rationale: Replaces defrost and power-level decisions with one obvious frozen-food action.
judge_comment: A single frozen-meal button is simple, but it is a common preset and the results will vary a lot with the meal.

title: No Power Knob Just Start
new_elements: Removed power knob (The oven always uses a safe medium power preset.)
rationale: Deleting the power knob removes an abstract setting that users must otherwise learn.
judge_comment: Removing the power knob simplifies operation and is easy to build, but many cheap microwaves already work this way and it isn't radical.

title: Fixed-Power Cycling
new_elements: Fixed 50 percent duty cycle (The magnetron always cycles at one gentle preset.)
rationale: Substitutes five power levels with one safe default, so there is nothing to choose.
judge_comment: A single fixed power level is simple and plausible but nearly duplicates idea 1, and it may heat poorly for some foods.

title: Rotary Phone Dial Timer
new_elements: Rotary dial timer (A finger-dial selects minutes and then springs back.)
rationale: Uses a pre-digital rotary-dial interaction familiar to older users for instant comprehension.
judge_comment: A rotary dial timer is a fun retro idea that older users will understand, though dialing a multi-digit time is slower and less intuitive for newer users.

title: Pull-Cord Minute Timer
new_elements: Pull-cord minute timer (Each pull adds exactly one minute to the cook time.)
rationale: Replaces numeric time entry with counting tugs, a more physical and obvious action.
judge_comment: A pull-cord that adds a minute per tug is a very simple, tactile and distinctive interaction, though long cook times need many pulls and a cord is a little awkward.

title: Twist Dial with Haptic Clicks
new_elements: Haptic detent dial (A single dial clicks through simple presets with tactile feedback.)
rationale: Substitutes two continuous knobs with guided clicks that users can feel and count.
judge_comment: A single detented preset dial is intuitive and easy to build, but dial-based microwaves are common and the preset choices are left undefined.

title: Big Red Cook Button
new_elements: Big red cook button (A single oversized button starts the default reheat cycle.)
rationale: Replaces timer setting with a universally understood big red start button.
judge_comment: A single start button directly removes the timer-setting learning curve, though one-touch start already exists and is not radical.

title: Big Blue Stop Button
new_elements: Big blue stop button (A single oversized button cancels and opens the door.)
rationale: Provides an obvious emergency exit without requiring timer or cancel knowledge.
judge_comment: An obvious stop is helpful, but most microwaves already have a stop or door-open stop, so it adds little to reducing the learning curve.

title: Door-Open Stops All
new_elements: Door-open auto stop (Opening the door instantly halts cooking and resets the cycle.)
rationale: Uses the natural act of opening the door as the only stop control needed.
judge_comment: Door-open stopping is already standard on all microwaves, so it is neither new nor a meaningful simplification.

title: Transparent RF Mesh Door
new_elements: Transparent conductive coated window (A coated glass pane blocks microwaves but remains clearer than perforated mesh.)
rationale: Replaces the hole-punched mesh with a clear pane so users can see food without visual clutter.
judge_comment: Transparent conductive coatings are plausible, but a clearer window barely affects ease of operation.

title: Microwave-Shielded Camera Display
new_elements: Microwave-shielded camera display (An internal camera shows food on an external screen with no window holes.)
rationale: Substitutes the entire see-through door with an always-clear screen view.
judge_comment: A shielded camera and screen is novel and concrete, but it adds cost and complexity and does little for the no-learning-curve need.

title: Full Transparent Faraday Cage
new_elements: Transparent metallic mesh film (A fine invisible mesh coats the whole cavity for see-through shielding.)
rationale: Replaces the perforated window with a fully transparent cage so checking food is effortless.
judge_comment: Transparent conductive mesh is plausible and novel, but it only marginally helps a no-learning-curve operation.

title: Larger Window No Lamp
new_elements: Larger unlit door window (A bigger clear window uses room light instead of an internal lamp.)
rationale: Substitutes the lamp and small window with one larger daylight view, reducing parts and confusion.
judge_comment: A larger window without a lamp is simple, but visibility suffers in dim rooms and shielding is harder, with little effect on operational learning.

title: Phosphorescent Cavity Liner
new_elements: Glow-in-the-dark cavity liner (The cavity glows softly after the lamp is removed.)
rationale: Replaces the interior lamp with passive glow so users can still see without operating a light.
judge_comment: Phosphorescent liner is quirky, but it would degrade with heat, grease and food, and would glow too dimly to be useful.

title: Door-Actuated LED Ring
new_elements: Door-actuated LED ring (Opening the door automatically turns on a simple ring light.)
rationale: Substitutes a separate lamp switch with automatic illumination tied to the door.
judge_comment: Door-triggered lighting is already standard, and it removes a manual step, so it is practical but not radical.

title: Omit Interior Lamp
new_elements: Omitted interior lamp (No lamp is fitted; the window and room light are sufficient.)
rationale: Removing the lamp removes another part and control, simplifying the product.
judge_comment: Removing the lamp is trivially feasible but is not novel, reduces usability, and barely addresses the need.

title: Mode Stirrer Kills Turntable
new_elements: Mode stirrer (A rotating metal paddle distributes microwaves without a turntable.)
rationale: Substitutes the turntable with a hidden stirrer so users never align or clean a plate.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist in some microwaves, so it is feasible but not radical, and it only modestly reduces operating effort.

title: Flat Ceramic Floor
new_elements: Flat ceramic floor (A fixed flat floor replaces the rotating glass turntable.)
rationale: Removes turntable placement as a user task, making loading the microwave obvious.
judge_comment: Flat-bed microwaves already exist and remove turntable concerns, but it is a modest, known substitution that does little for the operating interface.

title: Disposable Paper Liner
new_elements: Disposable microwave-safe liner (A drop-in liner catches splatter and is thrown away.)
rationale: Substitutes cleaning routines with a simple throwaway liner, reducing user decisions.
judge_comment: A disposable liner is plausible but addresses cleaning rather than operation, and adds a consumable.

title: One-Button Steam Clean
new_elements: One-button steam clean (A single button runs a fixed steam-cleaning cycle.)
rationale: Replaces manual cleaning with one obvious cycle that needs no settings.
judge_comment: A one-button steam clean is simple, but cleaning is peripheral to the core operation and similar features already exist.

title: Full-Width Door Handle
new_elements: Full-width door handle (A single long handle pulls the door open directly.)
rationale: Substitutes a small push button with a graspable handle, an action everyone knows.
judge_comment: A full-width handle is an intuitive, familiar affordance that is easy to build, but it is incremental and only covers opening the door.

title: Push-to-Open Spring Door
new_elements: Push-to-open spring door (Pressing the door itself releases a spring catch.)
rationale: Replaces the separate release button with the familiar push-to-open cabinet action.
judge_comment: Intuitive and cheap, but push-to-open is already used on some appliances, so it is not radical.

title: Foot Pedal Door Opener
new_elements: Foot pedal door opener (A floor-level pedal opens the door hands-free.)
rationale: Substitutes the hand button with a simple pedal that elderly users can operate without bending.
judge_comment: Hands-free opening is simple to use, but a floor pedal is awkward for a countertop microwave and adds mechanical complexity.

title: Kick-to-Open Door Plate
new_elements: Kick plate door release (A large lower plate opens the door with a gentle kick.)
rationale: Replaces dexterous button pressing with a gross motor action that is instantly clear.
judge_comment: Memorable and wild, but kicking a countertop appliance is impractical and risks damage or spills.

title: Voice Open Door
new_elements: Voice-actuated door latch (The single word Open releases the latch.)
rationale: Substitutes the physical release button with a spoken word already used daily.
judge_comment: Voice is a natural interface with no learning curve, but it adds cost and complexity instead of substituting something simpler.

title: Clap-On Clap-Off Cooking
new_elements: Clap sensor (One clap starts cooking and two claps open the door.)
rationale: Replaces knobs and buttons with a clap pattern that requires almost no instruction.
judge_comment: Playful and needs little instruction, but false triggers from noise and a lack of control over time and power limit it.

title: Single Motion Gesture Cook
new_elements: Wave-once gesture control (A single hand wave starts a fully automatic cook cycle.)
rationale: Substitutes all settings with one intuitive gesture, eliminating the control panel.
judge_comment: A one-wave start is very simple, but it doesn't explain how the oven knows what food it is cooking, so a fully automatic cycle is questionable.

title: Pop-Up Doneness Probe
new_elements: Pop-up thermometer probe (A probe pops up when food reaches temperature, ending cooking.)
rationale: Replaces timer cook cycles with a physical doneness signal familiar from meat thermometers.
judge_comment: A pop-up probe is a familiar cue, but a microwave cavity makes it hard to build, and the probe must be inserted into the food.

title: Reusable Thermal Probe
new_elements: Reusable doneness probe (A simple probe inserted into food stops the oven at temperature.)
rationale: Substitutes time-setting with inserting a probe, a one-step physical task.
judge_comment: Temperature-probe microwaves already exist, and inserting a probe adds a step, but the idea is plausible and fairly simple.

title: Color-Changing Cavity Wall
new_elements: Thermochromic cavity wall (The wall changes color as food heats, showing doneness without settings.)
rationale: Replaces numeric timers with a visual color cue that anyone can interpret.
judge_comment: A thermochromic wall is a novel idea, but the wall temperature doesn't reflect the food's doneness, and it can't stop the oven by itself.

title: Countdown Chime Only
new_elements: Bell-only timer (The timer has no display and simply rings when done.)
rationale: Substitutes a numeric countdown with an end bell, so users need only hear when it is done.
judge_comment: A bell-only timer is trivially feasible and simple, but it is not radical, and users still need to know how long to set.

title: One-Button AutoCook
new_elements: One-Button AutoCook Pad (Single large start pad replaces timer and power knobs.); Automatic Cook Cycle (Microwave senses load and runs a default safe cycle.)
rationale: One press replaces all programming decisions, so there is no learning curve.
judge_comment: Directly targets zero learning curve, but one-button start with load sensing is already common and the sensing mechanism is vague.

title: No Power Knob
new_elements: Fixed-Power Module (Removes the 5-step power knob entirely.); Preset Power Management (Internally applies safe duty cycles without user choice.)
rationale: Eliminating power choices removes a control users must understand.
judge_comment: Easy to build and removes one control, but it limits function and does not cover timing, so it only partly serves the need.

title: Pull-Open Magnetic Door
new_elements: Magnetic Door Seal (Door is held by magnets and opens by pulling.); No-Button Door Release (Door opens naturally without a push-release button.)
rationale: Users already know how to pull a door, so no button-learning is needed.
judge_comment: Pull-open doors with magnetic latches are familiar and plausible, though door release is a small part of the learning curve and safety interlocks must be handled.

title: Transparent No-Lamp Door
new_elements: Full-Clear Door Panel (Highly transparent shielded panel replaces viewing holes and lamp.); Daylight Viewing (Interior is visible without an internal light.)
rationale: No light button or lamp reliance means simpler checking of food.
judge_comment: Little connection to operating simplicity, and a fully clear door without a lamp is poor in dim kitchens and hard to shield against microwaves.

title: Auto-Stop Steam Sensor
new_elements: Steam Sensor (Detects steam and stops heating automatically.); Automatic Stop (No timer setting required for reheating.)
rationale: The microwave decides when food is hot, removing timer guesswork.
judge_comment: Steam sensors already exist in sensor-reheat models, but they do remove timer guesswork and the mechanism is clearly named.

title: Pictogram Food Dial
new_elements: Pictogram Dial (Dial shows pictures of common foods instead of minutes.); Picture-Based Selection (User points at the food type and presses start.)
rationale: Icons are instantly understood without reading or learning timings.
judge_comment: Easy to understand and cheap to build, but pictogram dials are a fairly incremental idea and food-type timing is imprecise.

title: Twist-Push Single Knob
new_elements: Twist-Push Knob (One knob twists for time and pushes to start.); Single-Control Operation (Replaces separate timer, power, and start controls.)
rationale: One physical control reduces the interface to a familiar twist-and-press.
judge_comment: Simple and feasible, but many microwaves already use a dial, so it is not radical.

title: Weight-Sensing One-Touch
new_elements: Base Weight Sensor (Weighs food placed on the turntable.); Weight-Based Auto Time (Sets cook time automatically from weight.)
rationale: Users need only place food and press one button; time is calculated for them.
judge_comment: Weight sensors exist and the one-button flow is simple, but weight alone does not capture food type or desired result, and the sensor adds cost.

title: Voice Cook Command
new_elements: Simple Voice Receiver (Recognizes only the phrase 'cook'.); Voice-Triggered Cooking (Starts a safe default cycle on command.)
rationale: Saying one word is simpler than navigating any control panel.
judge_comment: A single-word voice trigger is feasible and easy to use, but a fixed default cycle is limiting and it adds a voice component rather than substituting a cheaper one.

title: NFC Recipe Tag
new_elements: NFC Tag Reader (Reads a tag on food packaging.); Packaging-Set Cooking (Microwave sets itself from the tag.)
rationale: No manual settings are needed because the package tells the microwave what to do.
judge_comment: Packaging-driven settings remove all manual input, but they depend on packaging adoption and do not cover food without tags.

title: Gesture Wave Start
new_elements: Motion Gesture Sensor (Detects a simple hand wave.); Wave-to-Start (Starts cooking without touching controls.)
rationale: A wave is intuitive and requires no button memorization.
judge_comment: A wave start is easy to do, but it doesn't say what cook time or power is used, and it adds a sensor rather than substituting a part with something simpler.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Pull-Out Drawer Body (Replaces hinged door with a drawer.); Drawer Access (Open and close like a familiar kitchen drawer.)
rationale: Drawer interaction is already learned in kitchens, so no microwave-specific door skill is needed.
judge_comment: Microwave drawers already exist and are familiar to use, but they only address opening the door and not the controls, which is where the learning curve lies.

title: Foot Pedal Door
new_elements: Foot Pedal Release (A pedal opens the door.); Hands-Free Door Open (No need to find a push button with full hands.)
rationale: The foot pedal is a single obvious action with no panel learning.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is a simple mechanism, but it only helps with opening the door and does nothing to simplify the operating controls.

title: Kick-to-Open Door
new_elements: Kick Latch (A soft kick opens the door.); Impact Door Release (Replaces the push-release button with a robust latch.)
rationale: The action is physical and obvious, requiring no interface learning.
judge_comment: Kick-to-open is wild, but it risks damage and safety problems and does not make operation any simpler.

title: Auto-Start on Door Close
new_elements: Door-Close Sensor (Detects when the door is shut.); Close-to-Cook (Starts a preset cycle when the door closes.)
rationale: Closing the door is the only action needed, eliminating start-button confusion.
judge_comment: Starting a preset cycle when the door closes removes the start step entirely, so it directly delivers no-learning-curve use and is easy to build with a door switch.

title: Single Big Start Button
new_elements: Big Start Button (One oversized illuminated button.); Start-Only Control (No other programmable controls.)
rationale: A single obvious button eliminates any learning curve.
judge_comment: Very directly removes learning curve, but a one-button microwave already exists and it isn't radical; unclear how it determines cook time.

title: Food-Icon Preset Buttons
new_elements: Food-Icon Buttons (Three buttons with food pictures.); Preset Cooking (Each button runs a safe preset.)
rationale: Users choose a picture instead of interpreting power and time.
judge_comment: Pictorial presets are intuitive and easy to build, though common in existing products and not radical.

title: No Turntable Rotating Antenna
new_elements: Rotating Antenna (Antenna rotates instead of the food plate.); Even Heating Without Turntable (Food can stay still on a simple shelf.)
rationale: Users no longer need to place food on a turntable correctly.
judge_comment: Rotating antennas are real and replace the turntable, but turntable placement is a minor learning issue so relevance is modest.

title: Stationary Stirrer Fan
new_elements: Microwave Stirrer Fan (Fixed fan distributes microwaves.); Turntable-Free Heating (Removes rotating plate and its alignment task.)
rationale: No turntable means nothing to position or learn about.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are standard in many microwaves; feasible and concrete but little novelty and weak tie to the need.

title: Self-Stirring Bowl
new_elements: Self-Stirring Container (Bowl stirs food using microwave-safe mechanism.); Automatic Stirring (Replaces turntable and manual stirring.)
rationale: Users just put food in and press start, with no rotating plate to manage.
judge_comment: Self-stirring container is novel and could reduce user effort, but a microwave-safe stirring mechanism is hard and vaguely specified.

title: Magnetic Latch No Button
new_elements: Magnetic Latch (Simple magnetic catch replaces push-release.); Direct Door Pull (Door opens by pulling, like a refrigerator.)
rationale: Pulling a door is universally understood, so no button is needed.
judge_comment: Pull-to-open is intuitive and easy to build, but it only removes a button and is hardly radical.

title: Touch-to-Open Door
new_elements: Touch-Sensitive Door Edge (Light touch pops the door open.); Touch Release (Replaces mechanical push button.)
rationale: A touch anywhere on the edge is simpler than finding a small button.
judge_comment: Capacitive touch release is plausible, but accidental opens and the lack of an obvious affordance weaken the simplicity gain.

title: Bimetallic Timer Dial
new_elements: Bimetallic Timer Dial (Heat-based mechanical timer replaces clockwork.); Simple Timed Shutoff (Dial turns and shuts off after heat accumulates.)
rationale: The dial feels like a simple kitchen timer, requiring no clockwork understanding.
judge_comment: A bimetallic heat-based timer is quirky, but it is imprecise, inconsistent, and hard to apply to a microwave, where the heat is in the food and not in the cavity.

title: Sand Timer Dial
new_elements: Sand Timer Dial (Visual falling-sand timer replaces mechanical clock.); Visual Time Remaining (User sees time draining without numbers.)
rationale: Time is shown as a familiar draining sand gesture, not a numerical setting.
judge_comment: A visual sand timer is intuitive and eye-catching, but it is bulky and its running time cannot be set precisely.

title: Color-Zone Time Dial
new_elements: Color-Zone Dial (Dial has green-yellow-red cooking zones.); Zone-Based Time (User picks a zone rather than exact minutes.)
rationale: Color zones are immediately readable and avoid minute counting.
judge_comment: Color zones remove the need to count minutes and are easy to build, but they are coarse and the zone meanings are unclear.

title: Moisture Sensor Auto Power
new_elements: Moisture Sensor (Detects food moisture during heating.); Auto Power Adjustment (Microwave changes power without user input.)
rationale: Removing the power knob means users never need to learn power levels.
judge_comment: Moisture-sensing auto power is a real but existing feature (sensor cooking), so it serves the need well but is not radical, and it substitutes a sensor for the knob.

title: Thermal Sensor Auto Power
new_elements: Thermal Sensor (Reads surface temperature of food.); Temperature-Feedback Heating (Adjusts power to reach safe serving temperature.)
rationale: The microwave manages power itself, so the user only starts it.
judge_comment: IR surface temperature feedback removes power decisions and is plausible, though sensing through a microwave cavity and uneven heating make it harder.

title: RFID Packaging Auto-Set
new_elements: RFID Reader (Reads simple tags on ready meals.); Packaging-Driven Settings (Food package supplies time and power.)
rationale: No settings are required because the packaging does the programming.
judge_comment: Package tags that program the oven give true zero-setup for ready meals, but depend on industry adoption and do not cover non-packaged food.

title: Simplified Smart App
new_elements: One-Button App (Phone app has only a single 'Cook' button.); Remote One-Touch (Starts microwave with one tap.)
rationale: The app cannot be overcomplicated; it presents only one obvious action.
judge_comment: A one-button phone app adds a device and pairing steps, so it is arguably harder than a physical button and is not radical.

title: Any-Food Button
new_elements: Any-Food Button (A single button labeled with a plate icon.); Universal Reheat (Runs a safe reheating profile for most foods.)
rationale: One button covers the common case, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single universal button is very simple and easy to build, but it is close to existing Quick Start buttons and gives vague results for varied foods.

title: Reheat Defrost Cook Icons
new_elements: Tri-Icon Control (Three icons: reheat, defrost, cook.); Three-Preset Operation (Only three obvious cooking jobs.)
rationale: Three universally understood icons replace all manual programming.
judge_comment: Very simple and usable, but three-preset microwaves are common and not radical, and it lacks timing detail.

title: Twist-to-Zero Timer
new_elements: Twist-to-Zero Dial (Dial only turns one way to zero.); One-Way Timer (Cannot be set incorrectly; it always counts down.)
rationale: A one-way timer removes any possible confusion in operation.
judge_comment: A one-way countdown dial is intuitive and hard to misuse, but it resembles old mechanical timers and the 'twist to zero' name is a bit confusing.

title: Single More-Less Control
new_elements: More-Less Rocker (Two buttons: more and less.); Relative Adjustment (User adjusts only relative to default.)
rationale: Users need not understand absolute time or power, only more or less.
judge_comment: A relative more/less control reduces number entry, but it needs a sensible default and the user doesn't know what 'more' means for different foods.

title: Ambient Glow Interior
new_elements: Glow-in-Dark Chamber (Interior glows softly without a lamp.); Passive Visibility (Food is visible without switching on a light.)
rationale: No light control or lamp reliance keeps the experience simple.
judge_comment: Interior glow is mostly irrelevant to operation simplicity, and glow-in-the-dark material inside a microwave is of doubtful practicality and safety.

title: Camera and Outside Window
new_elements: Interior Camera (Camera displays food on outside window.); Indirect Viewing (Replaces holes and lamp with a screen.)
rationale: Users see inside at a glance without learning any new control.
judge_comment: A camera-and-screen view is novel but costly and complex, and it does not simplify operation, which runs against the SUBSTITUTE brief of cheaper or simpler parts.

title: Projected Doneness Indicator
new_elements: Doneness Projector (Projects a simple ready symbol on the counter.); Ambient Status Display (Shows when food is done without reading controls.)
rationale: A projected ready cue removes the need to interpret timer numbers.
judge_comment: A projected ready symbol is feasible but only helps end-of-cycle awareness, does not simplify operation, and adds parts rather than substituting cheaper ones.

title: No Clock Just Bell
new_elements: Bell-Only Feedback (Removes digital clock and display.); End-of-Cycle Bell (One sound signals completion.)
rationale: No clock means nothing to set or learn; the bell is universally understood.
judge_comment: Removing the clock simplifies the interface, similar to old mechanical timer microwaves, but it doesn't address how to set time or power.

title: Bell Replaced by Auto-Stop
new_elements: Silent Auto-Stop (Microwave simply stops without a bell.); No-Notification Shutoff (Removes bell mechanism and its sound.)
rationale: Fewer components and no ringing to interpret makes operation simpler.
judge_comment: A silent stop removes the completion cue and makes it worse for users, so it barely helps simplicity.

title: Door Window Replaced by Full Transparent Body
new_elements: Transparent Casing (Entire microwave body is see-through.); All-Angle Visibility (User sees food from any side without a door window.)
rationale: No specific viewing window or lamp is needed, reducing interaction learning.
judge_comment: A transparent body is unsafe because it leaks microwaves and has no link to learning curve.

title: Light Replaced by Electroluminescent Panel
new_elements: Electroluminescent Wall (Interior wall glows evenly without a bulb.); Built-In Illumination (No replaceable lamp or switch.)
rationale: Interior visibility is automatic, so users never manage a lamp.
judge_comment: Electroluminescent interior lighting is plausible and removes lamp management, but users already ignore the lamp, so it adds little to ease of use.

title: Mechanical Cam Replaced by Spring Timer
new_elements: Spring Timer (Simple spring-driven timer replaces clockwork cam.); Basic Countdown (Counts down and rings once.)
rationale: A spring timer is a familiar single-action control with no learning curve.
judge_comment: Mechanical dial timers are already how simple microwaves work, so it is highly feasible and intuitive but not radical.

title: Power Cam Replaced by Single Diode
new_elements: Single Diode Power Limiter (One diode sets a medium power.); Fixed Safe Power (Removes 5-step cam and its positions.)
rationale: No power choices means users cannot select the wrong setting.
judge_comment: Removing power choices simplifies use, but a single diode cannot realistically limit magnetron power to a medium level, and fixed power hurts function.

title: Door Release Replaced by Push-Push Latch
new_elements: Push-Push Latch (Push once to open, push again to close.); Toggle Door Action (Replaces separate release button.)
rationale: A push-push latch is a familiar furniture-style action with no button hunting.
judge_comment: Push-push latches are cheap and familiar, though the benefit to learning is modest and it is a small change.

title: Turntable Replaced by Rotating Antenna
new_elements: Rotating Antenna (Antenna spins under the food chamber.); Stationary Food Heating (Eliminates turntable plate and motor.)
rationale: Users can place any microwave-safe dish without aligning it to a turntable.
judge_comment: Rotating antennas or stirrers already exist in commercial microwaves, and they remove turntable concerns but add little to operation.

title: Turntable Motor Replaced by Convection Fan
new_elements: Convection Stirrer Fan (Fan circulates microwaves instead of rotating food.); Air-Based Even Heating (Removes turntable motor and plate.)
rationale: No turntable means no positioning step, reducing operation to open and close.
judge_comment: A stirrer fan is real technology, but the description conflates convection with microwave stirring and the link to ease of use is indirect.

title: Controls Replaced by Single Rotary Encoder
new_elements: Single Rotary Encoder (One knob controls everything.); Rotate-and-Press Operation (Turn to choose, press to confirm.)
rationale: A single knob-press interaction is easier to learn than multiple buttons.
judge_comment: Feasible and simpler than a keypad, but single-knob menus can add navigation complexity and similar designs already exist.

title: Control Panel Replaced by E-Ink Labels
new_elements: E-Ink Control Labels (Labels change to show only relevant options.); Adaptive Simple Labels (Only one or two choices appear at a time.)
rationale: Showing only the next possible action prevents overwhelming the user.
judge_comment: Adaptive labels reduce clutter, but changing labels may confuse users and add cost, so it is a modest substitution.

title: Knob Replaced by Dial with Detents
new_elements: Detented Dial (Dial clicks into a few discrete positions.); Click-Stop Selection (User feels each setting rather than reading it.)
rationale: Tactile detents make settings obvious without visual learning.
judge_comment: Tactile detents are intuitive and cheap, but this is a familiar mechanical approach with limited radicalness.

title: Timer Replaced by Countdown-to-Off
new_elements: Countdown-to-Off Knob (Knob only sets remaining time.); Immediate Countdown (No separate start button needed.)
rationale: Turning the knob starts the microwave, so there is no separate start step.
judge_comment: Turn-to-start timer is very intuitive and removes a step, though it mirrors classic mechanical microwaves.

title: Whole Interface Replaced by Open-Put-Close-Press
new_elements: Four-Action Interface (Only open, put, close, press remain.); Four-Step Simple Operation (All other controls are hidden and automatic.)
rationale: Reducing the entire experience to four obvious physical actions ensures no learning curve.
judge_comment: Strongly serves zero learning curve with automatic operation, but requires sensing food and power choice, which is technically challenging, and the mechanism is vague.
